 Union Govt notifies new airfare rules under Bharatiya Vayuyan Niyam, 2026
 By Surabhi Singh 
 November 2, 2026 
 Bharatiya Vayuyan Niyam, 2026 
 Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp 
 The central government has notified new rules that will allow it to step in over airline ticket prices during extraordinary situations and when intervention is considered necessary in the public interest. The move comes at a time when concerns over high airfares have grown because of elevated crude oil and Aviation Turbine Fuel, or ATF, prices. However, the government has not introduced a permanent cap on airfares; airlines will continue to decide ticket prices mainly according to market conditions.
 The new framework has been notified under the Bharatiya Vayuyan Niyam, 2026 by the Union Ministry of Civil Aviation. It was published in the Official Gazette on October 31 and will come into force from January 1, 2027. The key provision is Rule 192, which deals with tariffs charged by airlines operating scheduled air services.
 Under these rules, an airline will have to determine its fares after considering factors such as the cost of operations. It will also have to submit details of its tariffs to the Directorate General of Civil Aviation, in the form, manner and periodicity specified by the regulator. This means that the government will have a formal system to receive and monitor fare-related information from scheduled airlines.
 The most important change is the government’s power to issue written directions to airlines if it believes that an extraordinary situation has arisen and that action is needed in the public interest. Any such direction will have to be proportionate to the situation and will remain in force only for the period specified in the order. In simple terms, the government is not taking over everyday fare-setting, but it has kept a safeguard for situations where ticket prices may rise sharply and cause hardship to passengers.
 The rules do not define what will count as an “extraordinary situation,” nor do they set a specific price threshold for intervention. They also do not prescribe a permanent fare ceiling. This gives the government flexibility to respond to exceptional events, but it also means the exact circumstances for action will depend on the government’s assessment at the time.
 For passengers, the rules bring a stronger focus on transparency. Airlines will have to publish their fares on their websites and other digital platforms so that travellers can see the information more easily. During booking and on the ticket itself, airlines will need to clearly display the total amount payable by the passenger.
 Airlines will also have to provide a separate breakdown of the fare. This includes the base fare, taxes, fees, cancellation charges, refund conditions and any other applicable charges. The aim is to help passengers understand what they are actually paying for, rather than seeing only one final amount without clarity on its components.
 The new rules retain the broad policy of allowing market forces to determine airfares. In normal circumstances, airlines can price tickets according to demand, route competition, operating costs and other commercial factors. But the government’s intervention power acts as a regulatory lever for unusual conditions, such as sudden demand surges on particular routes or major disruptions that may lead to very high fares.
 For ordinary travellers, the practical benefit may be greater clarity and a safety valve during exceptional situations. A passenger booking a flight should be able to see the total cost and its breakdown more clearly, while the government can act temporarily if fares become unreasonable during a crisis. For airlines, the rules preserve pricing freedom but add clearer reporting, disclosure and monitoring obligations.
 Overall, the Bharatiya Vayuyan Niyam, 2026 strikes a balance between a market-based aviation pricing system and passenger protection. It does not promise permanently cheaper flights, but it creates a mechanism for temporary intervention, strengthens fare transparency and gives DGCA a continuing role in monitoring airline tariffs from January 1, 2027.
